title: Measuring HRV: protocol, devices and noise
goal: Set up a repeatable morning HRV routine, pick a device, and read it through a rolling mean, the CV and your own range.

steps.title: A morning routine you can repeat
steps.text:
The usual protocol is a short recording of 5–10 min on waking, in a quiet room, before the day's activity starts [[c:hm-morning]]. Both [supine](g:supine) and standing recordings are used in research. Supine is easier for athletes to do in the field; whether standing adds information is unclear [[c:hm-posture]].

What matters more than the choice is doing it the same way every time: same position, same time, same breathing. Mixed conditions add noise that looks like change.

Check the data too. One skipped or extra beat in a 5-min recording can shift common [HRV](g:hrv) indices by up to 50%, so edit the RR series or repeat the test [[c:hm-artifact]].

claims.text: Best practice for athletes is a short recording on waking in the morning.

evidence.quote: Currently, the best practice for athletes tends to be short-term (5–10 min) measurements of HR(V) upon awakening in the morning

claims.text: Supine is better tolerated in the field; the extra value of standing is unclear.

evidence.quote: the supine condition is better tolerated by athletes in the field
Whether the more constraining standing recordings reveal extra information compared with supine is unclear at the moment

claims.text: A single ectopic or skipped beat in a 5-min recording can change common HRV indices by up to 50%.

evidence.quote: the presence of a single ectopic beat (or a skipped beat) over a 5-min recording can modify common HRV indices up to 50%

steps.title: Chest strap or optical sensor?
steps.text:
A chest strap picks up the heart's electrical signal. Optical sensors ([PPG](g:ppg)) in phones, watches and rings read the pulse in the skin.

In 29 healthy adults at rest, smartphone PPG and a chest strap each agreed acceptably with [ECG](g:ecg) for [rMSSD](g:rmssd) (technical error about 6%) [[c:hm-ppg]]. Those were 5-min tests at rest, with guided and with normal breathing, so they cover the still morning test.

Overnight wearables are a different case. Across 536 nights in 13 adults, five devices differed in how well they matched ECG: Oura rings were closest for HRV, Garmin and Polar agreed less well [[c:hm-wear]]. Whichever you pick, keep the same device: a switch can look like a change in you.

claims.text: Smartphone PPG and a chest-strap sensor agree acceptably with ECG for resting rMSSD.

evidence.quote: Both PPG and heart-rate sensors provide an acceptable agreement for the measurement of rMSSD when compared with ECG.

claims.text: Accuracy of nightly HRV differs between consumer wearables.

evidence.quote: poor agreement from both Garmin (CCC = 0.87, MAPE = 10.52 ± 8.63%) and Polar (CCC = 0.82, MAPE = 16.32 ± 24.39%)

steps.title: One morning is noisy: average
steps.text:
Resting rMSSD varies by about 12% from day to day with nothing changing [[c:hm-cv]], so one reading is a poor guide. Take a [rolling mean](g:rolling-mean): the average of the last 7 mornings, updated daily.

How many mornings are needed? In trained triathletes, 3 randomly chosen valid days a week gave nearly the same picture as all 7 [[c:hm-3days]]. In another trial, one reading a week missed the autonomic changes of overreaching that the weekly mean caught [[c:hm-weekly]].

Aim for most mornings, accept at least 3 a week, and judge the trend, not the day.

claims.text: The day-to-day variation (CV) of rMSSD is about 12%.

evidence.quote: coefficient of variation (CV) for rMSSD ≈12% vs. low-to-high frequency oscillations ratio, LF/HF, CV ≈82%

claims.text: At least 3 valid readings per week are needed to monitor training with HRV.

evidence.quote: Practitioners using HRV to monitor training adaptation should use a minimum of 3 (randomly selected) valid data points per week.

claims.text: Isolated once-weekly recordings may miss autonomic change that weekly means detect.

evidence.quote: It also revealed that due to a wide day-to-day variability, isolated, once per week HRV recordings may not detect training-induced autonomic modulations in F-OR athletes.

steps.title: Updating a 7-day rolling mean
steps.problem: A runner's last 7 mornings of rMSSD are 66, 70, 68, 72, 64, 69 and 67 ms. Tomorrow's reading is 63 ms. What is the rolling mean now and tomorrow?
steps: Tomorrow the oldest value (66) leaves and 63 joins: 476 − 66 + 63 = 473; 473 ÷ 7 ≈ 67.6 ms.
Shortcut: new mean = old mean + (new − oldest) ÷ 7 = 68.0 + (63 − 66) ÷ 7 = 68.0 − 0.4 = 67.6 ms.
A bad morning (−5 ms against the mean) moved the average by less than 1 ms. That damping is the point.

steps.title: Spread: the CV of the week
steps.text:
The mean is one number. The other is how much the week bounces about: the [coefficient of variation](g:coefficient-of-variation) (CV) = [standard deviation](g:standard-deviation) ÷ mean × 100.

In a case study, the athlete heading for non-functional [overreaching](g:overreaching) showed a falling 7-day mean of [ln rMSSD](g:ln-rmssd) and a falling CV of the 7-day window, while the control stayed flat [[c:hm-cvfall]]. A shrinking CV can be a warning as well as a falling mean. It is a case study of two athletes, so treat it as a lead, not a rule.

(The paper worked out the CV on ln rMSSD. Logs squeeze the spread, so a CV on ln values comes out much smaller than one on ms: compare a CV only with CVs worked out the same way. The examples here use ms.)

claims.text: In one overreached triathlete, both the 7-day mean and the week-to-week variation of HRV fell before the poor race.

evidence.quote: These data suggest that trends in both absolute HRV values and day-to-day variations may be useful measurements indicative of the progression towards mal-adaptation or non-functional over-reaching.

steps.title: CV of a week
steps.problem: A runner's morning rMSSD over 7 days: 62, 70, 66, 58, 72, 64, 68 ms. Find the mean and the CV.
steps: Variance with n − 1 = 6: 139.4 ÷ 6 ≈ 23.2 ms². SD = √23.2 ≈ 4.8 ms.
CV = 4.8 ÷ 65.7 × 100 ≈ 7.3%. This week bounced less than the typical day-to-day CV of rMSSD, about 12%.

steps.title: Is this change big enough?
steps.text:
Judge the 7-day mean against your own range, not a population norm: levels differ by age, sex and recording length, and your noise is yours alone.

Trials set that range from the athlete's own history. Kiviniemi used the 10-day mean minus one SD (of [HF power](g:hf-power)); Vesterinen used an individually determined [smallest worthwhile change](g:smallest-worthwhile-change) [[c:hm-band-def]]. A reading inside the band counts as normal; one below it, or a downward trend over days, counts as low.

Two habits keep it honest: build the baseline over a few weeks of normal training before using it, and re-set it as fitness changes.

claims.text: Trials set a personal reference range from the athlete's own recent readings.

evidence.quote: If there was significant decrease in HRV (below reference value [10-day mean-SD] or decreasing trend for 2 days), low-intensity training or rest was prescribed.
The MOD/HIT session was programmed if HRV was within an individually determined smallest worthwhile change.

points: Measure for 5–10 min on waking, in the same position, at the same time, with the same breathing; edit or repeat if a beat is missed.
Chest straps and phone PPG agree acceptably with ECG at rest; overnight wearables differ by brand. Keep one device.
One morning varies by about 12%: use a 7-day rolling mean, with at least 3 valid mornings a week.
The CV of the week shows the bounce: a shrinking CV together with a falling mean was a warning in a case study.
Judge changes against your own range (for example 10-day mean minus one SD, or your smallest worthwhile change), not a population norm.

variants.stem: A runner records HRV lying down at 7:00 on Monday, standing after coffee on Tuesday, and lying down at 9:00 after walking the dog on Wednesday. What is the main problem?

options.text: Position, timing and activity all changed, so shifts may not reflect recovery
options.why: Right: standard conditions are what make day-to-day changes interpretable.

options.text: Lying down is not valid for rMSSD
options.why: Supine is common and better tolerated in the field.

options.text: Recordings shorter than 10 minutes cannot be used
options.why: 5–10 min is the usual length for athletes.

options.text: He should only measure after training, when fatigue shows
options.why: The standard protocol is the morning on waking, not after training.

variants.stem: A cyclist uses paced breathing on race weeks and normal breathing in training weeks. His HRV 'jumps' every race week. What is the best explanation?

options.text: His vagus is more active before races
options.why: That can be true, but a change in breathing alone can produce the jump, so remove it first.

options.text: Chest straps are less accurate on race weeks
options.why: Nothing links device accuracy to race weeks.

options.text: The change in breathing between weeks adds a difference that is not recovery
options.why: Right: breathing pace changes RSA, so conditions need to match.

options.text: Race-week readings should be thrown out as outliers
options.why: They are real readings; the protocol is what needs fixing.

variants.stem: A triathlete's 5-min strap recording shows an rMSSD of 120 ms, double his usual 60 ms. The trace shows one large spike, a missed beat. What should he do?

options.text: Log it as a huge recovery boost and train hard today
options.why: One artefact can double rMSSD; it may not be real.

options.text: Edit out the missed beat or repeat the test before trusting it
options.why: Right: a single bad beat can shift HRV indices by up to 50%.

options.text: Delete the whole week's readings to be on the safe side
options.why: One bad beat does not spoil the other days.

options.text: Switch to standing recordings from now on
options.why: Posture is not the cause; a missed beat is.

variants.stem: A runner's morning rMSSD is 38 ms against a usual 70 ms. The trace shows one extra beat early in the recording. What is the best step?

options.text: Rest today: a 46% drop is a clear sign of overreaching
options.why: The drop may come from the artefact.

options.text: Average it with the next three days without checking
options.why: Averaging keeps the error in the data.

options.text: Replace rMSSD with LF/HF, which is not affected
options.why: Ratios are noisier; the fix is clean data.

options.text: Correct the extra beat or repeat the recording, then read the value
options.why: Right: one ectopic or extra beat can distort rMSSD by up to 50%.

variants.stem: A cyclist wants daily HRV. Option 1 is a chest strap with a phone app each morning; option 2 is a smartwatch's overnight HRV. What does the evidence support?

options.text: Optical sensors cannot measure HRV at all in practice
options.why: In a resting test, phone PPG agreed acceptably with ECG.

options.text: Any wearable's overnight HRV is as accurate as ECG
options.why: Five devices differed: some agreed poorly.

options.text: Both can work, but device quality varies, so check the model and keep one device
options.why: Right: strap and PPG agreed with ECG at rest, while overnight wearables differed by brand.

options.text: Chest straps are valid only during exercise
options.why: The strap was validated at rest for rMSSD.

variants.stem: A runner switches from a Polar strap to a ring in week 6 and sees her HRV 'improve' by 15% with no change in training. What is the likeliest explanation?

options.text: Different devices read HRV differently, so a switch can look like a real change
options.why: Right: keep one device or re-set the baseline after a switch.

options.text: The ring detects extra vagal activity that the strap misses
options.why: The sensor cannot detect vagal activity the heart does not produce; it just reads the pulse differently.

options.text: Her fitness jumped 15% in one night
options.why: Nothing in the training supports that.

options.text: Rings are more accurate than ECG
options.why: ECG is the reference; no consumer device beats it.

variants.stem: Against ECG, one wearable's nightly HRV has a mean absolute error of about 6% (Oura Gen 4: 5.96%), another's about 16% (Polar: 16.32%). Normal day-to-day spread is about 12%. Which statement is best?

options.text: Both are fine: any error under 20% is acceptable
options.why: An error larger than the day-to-day spread swamps small real changes.

options.text: 6% is small beside the 12% spread; 16% is larger and could hide a real change
options.why: Right: device error should be well below the signal you want to see.

options.text: Neither can be used, since both have some error
options.why: A 6% error is small against a 12% spread; some error is expected.

options.text: The 16% device is better because it reports more variation
options.why: More variation from error is noise, not information.

variants.stem: A cyclist's 7-day rolling mean of rMSSD is 68 ms. The reading from 7 days ago (leaving the window) was 72 ms and today's is 65 ms. What is the new rolling mean?

options.why: This replaces the mean with today's value, ignoring the other six days.
This averages the old and new values, (72 + 65) ÷ 2, instead of updating the mean.
This subtracts the full 7 ms change without dividing by 7.

variants.solution: New mean = old mean + (new − oldest) ÷ 7 = 68 + (65 − 72) ÷ 7 = 68 − 1 = 67.0 ms.

variants.stem: A runner's 7-day mean is 60 ms. The value leaving the window is 66 ms and today's reading is 63 ms. What is the new mean?

options.why: This replaces the mean with today's value.
This averages the leaving and new values, (66 + 63) ÷ 2.
This subtracts the full 3 ms without dividing by 7.

variants.stem: A triathlete's 7-day mean is 75 ms. The leaving value is 70 ms and today's is 80 ms. What is the new mean?

options.why: This replaces the mean with today's value.
This ignores today's change altogether.
This adds the full 10 ms without dividing by 7.

variants.stem: In trained triathletes, what is the fewest valid morning HRV readings per week worth averaging?

options.why: Right: 3 randomly chosen valid days gave nearly the same picture as all 7.
One reading a week missed the changes that weekly means caught.
Five is a good aim but not the minimum; gains plateaued after 3–4 days.
Daily is ideal but not the minimum.

variants.stem: A runner measures HRV only on Sunday mornings. Over three weeks: 68, 59, 71 ms. He decides he was overreached in week 2. What is the best comment?

options.text: He is right: any drop on a recording day signals overreaching
options.why: The 13% drop is about the size of ordinary day-to-day variation.

options.text: One reading varies about 12% alone and 59 is only 13% below 68: add more mornings
options.why: Right: one reading per week cannot separate a real change from ordinary day-to-day noise.

options.text: He is wrong: HRV cannot show overreaching in anybody
options.why: Weekly means of HRV did detect changes in overreached athletes.

options.text: He should use only the highest value of the week
options.why: The mean of several days is the steadier choice.

variants.solution: (59 − 68) ÷ 68 × 100 = −13.2%. Typical day-to-day variation of rMSSD is about 12%.

variants.stem: A cyclist records HRV on 1 morning each week: 80, 70, 82 ms. She cuts her training after the 70. What is the main flaw?

options.text: A 12.5% dip is normal day-to-day spread, so one reading a week proves little
options.why: Right: add more mornings, then judge the rolling mean.

options.text: Training should never be changed on HRV data alone
options.why: HRV can inform training when used on a rolling basis.

options.text: The later 82 ms reading proves the 70 was a mistake
options.why: A later higher value does not prove the earlier one wrong; the noise is normal.

options.text: Only a chest strap can detect a change as small as 12%
options.why: Device type does not change the problem.

variants.stem: A cyclist's morning rMSSD over 7 days: 55, 61, 58, 52, 64, 57, 59 ms (mean 58.0 ms, sample SD 3.9 ms). What is the CV?

options.why: This is the SD in ms, not divided by the mean and put on a percent scale.
This divides the squared deviations by n (7) instead of n − 1 (6), shrinking the SD.
This uses the range (12 ms) divided by the mean, not the SD.

variants.stem: A runner's 7 mornings: 48, 54, 50, 44, 56, 52, 46 ms (mean 50.0 ms, sample SD 4.3 ms). What is the CV?

options.why: This is the SD in ms, not divided by the mean.
This divides by n instead of n − 1 when finding the SD.
This uses the range (12 ms) divided by the mean.

variants.stem: A triathlete's 7 mornings: 80, 74, 86, 78, 90, 76, 82 ms (mean 80.9 ms, sample SD 5.6 ms). What is the CV?

options.why: This is the SD in ms, not divided by the mean.
This divides by n instead of n − 1 when finding the SD.
This uses the range (16 ms) divided by the mean.

variants.stem: A triathlete's 7-day mean of rMSSD is stable, but the CV of the week has halved over 3 weeks while her training volume rises. What is the best response?

options.text: Ignore it: only the mean of the week matters here
options.why: The case study found variation changing too.

options.text: Celebrate: less variability always means better recovery
options.why: A flat, low-variation pattern preceded overreaching in that case.

options.text: Treat it as a possible warning: check sleep, mood and a standard session
options.why: Right: in one case study, shrinking variation came before non-functional overreaching; it is a lead, not proof.

options.text: Stop training completely for two weeks right away
options.why: One weak signal does not justify a long break; check the other measures.

variants.stem: A runner's 7-day CV of rMSSD drops from 9% to 4% over a hard block, with the mean unchanged. What is the soundest next step?

options.text: Take it as proof that she is now overreached
options.why: Two athletes cannot prove it.

options.text: Treat it as a possible warning; check wellness and a standard effort
options.why: Right: the pattern appeared before overreaching in a two-athlete case study, so use it as a prompt to look further.

options.text: Ignore it because the mean has not changed at all
options.why: Both mean and variation were suggested as useful in the case study.

options.text: Double the training load to push through the block
options.why: Adding load on a possible warning is the wrong direction.

variants.stem: Why compare today's HRV with your own range instead of a published population norm?

options.text: Population norms are always wrong
options.why: They are fine for what they cover; they just do not tell you your own normal.

options.text: Norms depend on recording length, age and sex, and your noise is yours alone
options.why: Right: only your own history shows what is unusual for you.

options.text: A personal range is not needed if you average 7 days
options.why: The average still needs your own range to judge against.

options.text: Norms only exist for SDNN
options.why: Norms exist for several indices; recording length and person still matter.
